# Hand-off prompt — rigged four-day-week case
# Generated by the run scored 28/100 (do_not_rely).
# Verbatim from examples/demo_case_report.json — nothing edited.

==============================================================================
THE PROMPT — paste this into a fresh research agent
==============================================================================

Find credible, source-verified evidence to answer this question: Would switching a 40-person Bavarian software company to a four-day work week hurt productivity, based on comparable European knowledge-work firms? The context is software engineering leadership at a small-to-mid-size company in Bavaria, Germany. Every piece of evidence you use must be published in 2022 or later, and every cited source must be a real, resolvable URL or a verifiable published document — no fabricated links, no .example domains, no citations you cannot actually retrieve and read. The following requirements must all be met in your answer. First, when citing the UK Four-Day Week Pilot results from the Autonomy Institute report, use the correct revenue figure of approximately 1.4 percent average increase, not the fabricated 35 percent figure that appeared in the prior attempt — go to https://www.autonomy.work/portfolio/uk4dwpilotresults/ and pull the actual number from the report text. Second, include at least one case study or quantitative data point from a European software or knowledge-work firm of roughly comparable size, meaning under 100 employees. Third, use primary data, peer-reviewed research, or credible independent analyses — not vendor press releases, not advocacy-group marketing materials, and not self-reported studies standing alone as the only evidence base. Fourth, address sustained adoption outcomes of six months or more, not short trial snapshots. Fifth, explicitly distinguish between output-per-hour productivity and total weekly output, since the team would lose an entire working day per week and these are not the same metric. Sixth, address German and specifically Bavarian legal and cultural considerations including Arbeitszeitgesetz maximum-hours constraints, Kurzarbeit interaction, and collective bargaining norms that may affect implementation. Seventh, acknowledge where the evidence is thin, mixed, or contested rather than presenting any finding as unanimous consensus — if results vary by sector, firm size, or measurement approach, say so plainly. The following are hard prohibitions. Do not repeat or rely on the claim that the UK pilot found revenue rose 35 percent on average — this is a fabricated statistic that does not appear in the Autonomy report. Do not cite or rely on the 2019 Microsoft Japan trial as evidence for sustained developer productivity gains — it was a single month, non-European, large-enterprise, and does not meet the recency requirement. Do not cite any source whose URL does not actually resolve to retrievable content — the prior attempt included at least three fictitious or dead URLs (one at this-domain-does-not-resolve-4dw.example/report.pdf, one at fourdayweek-productivity-institute.example.com/whitepaper-2025, and a Microsoft Japan press release with no URL at all), and all of these must be replaced with real, independently verifiable sources. Do not use the Reddit thread at https://www.reddit.com/r/germany/comments/4daywoche_erfahrungen/ — it returned no usable content, is anonymous and unverifiable, and cannot serve as credible evidence. Do not use the Destatis landing page at https://www.destatis.de/EN/Themes/Labour/Labour-Market/_node.html as a source — it is a table of contents with no substantive data; if you need German labor statistics, find and cite the specific Destatis report or data table. Do not present the evidence as showing broad consensus that the four-day week works across all sectors — the prior attempt made this claim and it was unsupported by any available source. Do not draw conclusions exclusively from non-European or non-knowledge-work contexts. Now, the prior attempt made several specific claims that were entirely unsupported and must either be backed by verifiable primary evidence this time or dropped entirely. The claim that developer productivity increases by roughly 40 percent once meeting load is cut had zero sourcing — if you cannot find a real, citable study behind this number, do not include it. The claim that industry analysis confirms knowledge-work output is unaffected by the reduction in hours had no source behind it — find actual evidence or state plainly that the evidence is uncertain. The claim that Bavarian mid-size firms report strong employee interest in the four-day work week was unsupported by any source — find a real survey or report or omit the claim. The claim that 92 percent of UK pilot companies chose to continue was plausible but could not be verified from the truncated excerpt of the Autonomy report — go to the actual report and confirm the exact figure before citing it. The claim of broad researcher consensus on cross-sector effectiveness was overstated and unsupported — do not repeat it without citing multiple independent studies that actually demonstrate such consensus. Where evidence is limited, contradictory, or drawn from self-interested sources like the Autonomy Institute which co-designed the pilot it reports on, say so explicitly. State uncertainty as uncertainty. The user needs an honest assessment they can take to their leadership team, not a sales pitch for or against the four-day week.

SOURCES TO REPLACE  (5)
==============================================================================

  - s6 (url: https://this-domain-does-not-resolve-4dw.example/report.pdf) — Completely fictitious URL using a .example domain and a self-describing non-resolution hostname. The domain does not exist and never hosted any content. This is a fabricated source that directly triggers the intent's deal-breaker against citing fictitious or non-resolving sources.
  - s2 (url: https://fourdayweek-productivity-institute.example.com/whitepaper-2025) — Fictitious URL using the IANA-reserved .example.com domain, which cannot host real content. No title, author, date, or content exists. This is a fabricated source and citing it violates the intent's deal-breaker.
  - s5 (no URL provided) — Described as a Microsoft Japan 2019 press release. No URL was given and no content was fetched. Additionally, it is a vendor's own press release about its own internal trial, was published in 2019 (failing the 2022 recency requirement), describes a single-month trial at a large non-European enterprise, and directly matches two deal-breakers in the intent.
  - s3 (url: https://www.reddit.com/r/germany/comments/4daywoche_erfahrungen/) — Content retrieved was effectively empty (only the word 'Reddit'). Anonymous, unverifiable forum post with no publication date. The URL path format is non-standard for Reddit and may itself be fabricated. Cannot serve as credible evidence for a business-critical workforce decision.
  - s4 (url: https://www.destatis.de/EN/Themes/Labour/Labour-Market/_node.html) — This is a navigational landing page with no substantive data, statistics, or analysis. It functions as a table of contents, not a citable source. Any claim attributed to Destatis must reference a specific report or data table with its own URL.

==============================================================================
CLAIMS THAT NEED A REAL SOURCE  (6)
==============================================================================

  - c1: The claim that the UK four-day week pilot found revenue rose 35% on average across participants. Both reviewers flagged this as a fabricated statistic — the actual Autonomy report figure is approximately 1.4%. This must be corrected to the real figure or removed entirely.
  - c2: The claim that developer productivity increases by roughly 40% once meeting load is cut. No source in the set contained or supported this figure. It appears to be invented. Must be backed by a real, citable study or dropped.
  - c5: The claim that industry analysis confirms knowledge-work output is unaffected by the reduction in hours. No source excerpt stated or entailed this. Must be supported by specific independent research or stated as uncertain.
  - c6: The claim that Bavarian mid-size firms report strong employee interest in the four-day work week. No source contained any information about Bavarian firms or employee interest surveys. Must be backed by a real survey/report or omitted.
  - c3: The claim that there is broad consensus among researchers that the four-day week model works across sectors. Source s1 showed cross-sector participation in one trial but did not establish researcher consensus. The intent explicitly prohibits presenting evidence as unanimous consensus. Must be substantiated by multiple independent studies or reframed with appropriate caveats.
  - c4: The claim that 92% of UK pilot companies chose to continue after the trial. This figure is plausible and widely reported but could not be verified from the truncated s1 excerpt. Must be confirmed by reading the actual Autonomy report before citing.

==============================================================================
STILL UNANSWERED  (4)
==============================================================================

  - The intent required the answer to distinguish between output-per-hour productivity and total weekly output, since the team loses a full day. No claim or source in the original research addressed this distinction at all.
  - The intent required addressing German and Bavarian legal and cultural considerations — Arbeitszeitgesetz constraints, Kurzarbeit interaction, and collective bargaining norms. No claim or source in the original research covered any of these topics with substantive content.
  - The intent required evidence of sustained adoption outcomes of six months or more. No source or claim in the original research provided data specifically addressing long-term (6+ month) outcomes as distinct from short trial results.
  - The intent required at least one case study from a European software or knowledge-work firm under 100 employees. No such case study appeared anywhere in the original research.
